title: Mindfulness Seminar 2
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett opens the second week of a six-week mindfulness seminar by hearing participants report on the body scan, then reads from the Satipatthana Sutta in Bhikkhu Bodhi's translation. Nomon outlines the sutra's four foundations of mindfulness and the six groups of body practices Thich Nhat Hanh finds in it, and offers three qualities from its repeated formula: ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful. After a lying-down movement practice, Nomon suggests home work with a yoga recording and the five daily recollections of decay, disease, and death. One option is to recite them quietly in a graveyard, including at a child's grave.

What exactly is the space that the body is taking up?
What exactly is the position of the body?
And what happens when we notice this very simple fact of our existence?
We notice the body and notice the breathing.

Thank you everybody.
I appreciate everybody's reports and I hope that no one felt too put on the spot.
So several of you mentioned yoga.
So you're in luck.
I thought we would do some yoga a little bit later.
But first, a little more from the Buddha.
This foundational sutra that we're getting our material from, directly or indirectly, the [unclear: "Satibhatana"] Sutra, is the sutra on mindfulness.
Sati means mindfulness.
It brings up four general areas for the study of mindfulness.
Some of you heard this, but it's worth repeating.
It seems to be implied, the commentaries say, that you should do them more or less in order.
A lot of times in Buddhism things are in a list and actually it's not necessarily a great idea to stick to that order, but in this case it sounds like it's good to go in the order.
The four areas that the Buddha brings up are, first, the body, and the body includes the breathing, so all the physical processes.
That's the first one.
There are several aspects of that, which I'll mention in a moment.
The second one that you mentioned is mindfulness of something called Vedana in Sanskrit, which the best translation is probably feeling tone.
They often translate this as feelings, which sounds like emotions, happy, sad, whatever, but feeling tone is better.
It's a little more of a basic feeling about our life or about any phenomenon that arises, the way we tend to lean towards things, push away from things, in a very low-level, subconscious way.
They often divide it into pleasant sensation, unpleasant sensation and neutral sensation.
So that's the second thing he suggested that we be mindful of.
That's like below thinking, before thinking.
But then thinking is included, actually, so the third foundation of mindfulness is mindfulness of thought and emotion.
Although in Buddhist psychology they don't break out emotion the way we do.

So the practice is to accurately observe thoughts and emotional states as they arise, as objects in the mind, [unclear: "which implode"], and the ability to do that, or even gaining the ability to do that, you can see an obvious benefit to that.
If I can observe angry thoughts arising, that puts me in a whole different relationship to those thoughts, you know what I mean?
A whole different mode with those thoughts.
I may still be angry in some way, but maybe not quite so possessed by that anger, or so identified with that anger.
So that's the third one, thought and emotion, and the fourth one is a pretty broad category The first and fourth are very broad categories.
The fourth one, I guess you could translate, is mindfulness of phenomena.
What that means is being able to analyze and understand the phenomena that arise in our life, I don't want to say through a filter, but with the tools of Buddhist teachings.
So the fourth one gets into all kinds of different Buddhist analyses of how things go for us.
It talks about things like the seven factors of enlightenment and the five hindrances and all kinds of stuff, so we'll get to that later in the seminar.
I just want to give you a broad sense of the context this is operating in.
Here's how it's weighted in the sutra.
The more literal translation of the sutra I have is 30 pages long in English.
First there's a one-page introduction, then nine pages about mindfulness of the body: lots of different practices and different ways to study the body, study the breathing.
So nine pages on the first foundation, one page on the second foundation, feeling tone, and one page on mindfulness of thought and emotion.
So that's important thinking, in the Buddhist point of view.
For us it's like everything, right?
The Buddha is like, "Come on."
Then there's a bunch of pages at the very end, 19 pages, on this mindfulness of phenomena through the vehicle of Dharma teachings, but that has to explicate a lot of stuff.
Then there's a one-page conclusion.
The point is that the Buddha put a great emphasis on mindfulness of the body, and what a great support that is for us.
Maybe all human beings are like this, but it does seem like our culture is extra super duper cerebral and thought-based.
What can you send down the wires of the internet but thoughts and concepts, right?
One thing that's interesting about these sutras is that you look at different translations and they have sections and headings and subsections, and it seems organized.
But actually the original sutras are nothing but a series of words from start to end.
There are no headers, no sections, no pages.
Those were all added later by translators and by the consensus of the commentary.

The reason I mention that is that Thich Nhat Hanh, who did one of the translations that I've been studying, in his book Transformation and Healing, analyzes the first section on mindfulness of the body.
I'll try to remember to leave these out tonight if you want to look at them.
He comes up with six ways that the Buddha suggests; he groups it into six groups of teachings from the Buddha on how to be mindful of the body.
I want to mention what those six groups are.
First there's mindfulness of the breath, which is then further explicated in four different ways.
The second thing the Buddha mentions is mindfulness of the positions of the body: standing, walking, sitting down.
The third is mindfulness of the actions of the body, so actually noticing what's happening when the body is in action, which is of course all the time.
Fourth is mindfulness of the parts of the body, so there's our body scan.
The fifth is mindfulness of the elements that form the body.
We could look at that in a scientific way, in terms of chemicals and molecules, and that would be fine: proteins, different tissues.
But the way it's explained in the sutra is to study the body in terms of the four traditional elements that constituted reality in Hindu philosophy: air, water, heat and earth, fire and earth.
The last is mindfulness of the impermanence and the decomposition of the body.
Actually this is a great long section, which sometimes I like to read out loud to kind of freak us out.
It's very detailed: you go to the charnel grounds, and you look for decomposing bodies in different states, and you practice this way with the body that's decomposed this much.
It's great stuff, but it could be in a way less culturally appropriate for us.
We have body image issues which mainly they didn't have then.
But we'll get to mindfulness of the decomposition of the body and practice with it in our context.

The body farm?
The body what?
There's a body farm at the University of North Carolina, I think.
Anyway, people volunteer their bodies, and they put them in different conditions and watch how they decompose, so that you can tell later, if they come up on a body, what might have happened.
It's becoming more accepted in the study of forensics.
Obviously Buddha was doing it for spiritual reasons, to accept the impermanence of the body, but I think it's fascinating forensically too.
So anyway.
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** There really is a strange exhibit from China, bodies.
Yeah.
Has anybody seen that?
Yeah, I guess.
Have you seen it?
It's in Seattle, I guess.
They've preserved bodies in different cross-sections and taken apart and stuff like that.
Yeah, and where the bodies came from, I guess, is a little bit suspect in China, but still it's parts, elements and impermanence.
Any one of these could be a lengthy study.
It would be worth doing; it would be worth putting time into practicing directly with any of these aspects of mindfulness of the body.
So far we've been looking at parts and, to a lesser extent, positions.
Sometimes you make notes and then later you look at them.
Let's hear a little bit of the sutra, then we'll do some awareness of positions of the body, do some practice, and I have some suggestions for you for home practice for the next week.
This is actually a different translation than I knew about.
I forgot to bring the book.
This is the translation by Bhikkhu Bodhi.
…in a wonderful collection of early Buddhist teachings called In the Buddha's Words, in the mind chapter.
It's a little more abbreviated translation, but he's one person I really would trust to do a short translation.
"Thus have I heard."
The idea here is that these teachings were preserved orally, so they always start with this sort of statement: "I heard this."
*Thus have I heard.
On one occasion there was a town of the Kurus named* [unclear: "Kama Samdhama"].
So these teachings happened in very particular places.
*And there he addressed the monks: "Monks."
"Venerable sir," they replied, and the Blessed One said: "Monks, this is the only way, the path for the purification of beings,"*
So what I'm about to do starts with a punch line.

*"this is the only way, the path for the purification of beings, for the surmounting of sorrow and lamentation, for the passing away of pain and dejection, for the attainment of the true way, for the realization of nirvana, namely the four establishments of mindfulness."*
So there's a key, but Bhikkhu Bodhi thinks it doesn't mean exactly that.
It's not the only way, there are many ways, but this way is effective in going forward.
If you practice mindfulness, there will be some progress towards these goals: purification, reducing of suffering, and nirvana.
That's a way that has traction.
What are the four?
The Buddha goes on.
*Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having subdued pain and rejection in regard to the world.*
Having subdued, let's type something here.

*Having subdued pain and rejection in regard to the world, he dwells contemplating, here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating, clearly comprehending and mindful,* three instructions there, *having subdued pain and rejection in regard to the world.
And he dwells contemplating feelings in the feelings, ardent, clearly comprehending and mindful, having subdued pain and rejection in regard to the world.
And he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending and mindful, having subdued pain and rejection in regard to the world.*
So there's some repetition here.
*And he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending and mindful, having subdued pain and rejection in regard to the world.
Here a monk, gone to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, sits down, having folded her legs crosswise, straightened her body, and established mindfulness in front of her.
Just mindful she breathes in, mindful he breathes out.
Breathing in long, he breathes out long.*
It continues like that for a while, talking about breathing and then talking about all these other areas that Thich Nhat Hanh listed for us.
But there are two or three things I want to highlight about this.
First, there is some attention and instruction given to having productive and supportive conditions for practice: sit at the foot of a tree or in a quiet hut.
Sometimes we understand that practice, to be really helpful, has to be all the time.
It's not only some special thing you do off some place.
But the Buddha is saying pretty clearly that you also do need formal practice, and to practice we put a ton of energy into this place because we recognize that.
The other thing I want to mention briefly is about these three points that he brought up in this repeated formula.
Repetition is common and important in Buddhist teachings.

It's interesting: in Buddhist teachings we say it a slightly different way for emphasis and to keep them interested, and because this is like, "No, if this is important, it's worth saying four times, and it's worth saying four times exactly the same."
So I mentioned what Bhikkhu Bodhi translated: in each of these, in general, whether we can bring up these three qualities.
First, ardent.

It's a little bit of an old-fashioned word, I guess, but it means a sort of firm resolve, gentle energy, but energy, bringing up energy: [unclear: "let this floor schlep into the cushion"] to sort of set the timer, and then we'll…
The second was clearly comprehending.
Comprehension, to us, has a sort of intellectual gloss, but it doesn't mean intellectual exactly.
It means knowing why we're doing what we're doing, or you could say having a clear intention.
So you could say understanding or intention there: why, in this moment?
But some feeling, some sense, some sort of direct directionality, like "This is important to my life, that's why I'm doing it."
And mindful.
This is also really common in Buddhism: how do you do mindfulness mindfully?

Sutras are famous for spending many hundreds of words saying all kinds of stuff, and then towards the end they say, "And what is this sutra about?" and then they tell you, or they say it at the beginning.
Anyway, it's a circular kind of thing, which is helpful to us because we think, "Oh, it should be sort of linear steps towards a goal."
So to bring in mindfulness, to be mindful, is to actually hold the awareness in a particular way, like we've been talking about.
Actually, one more point I want to make is this point about dwelling.
There's a sense in these teachings of immersion.
Not to hold this at arm's length, as something to sort of try over here, but to enter into it fully with the whole body and mind.
As I sit down to sit, as I lie down to the body scan, I'm just sinking into this, immersing myself in this for this time, dwelling here, really living in this practice for this time.
Okay, so as we go along these four weeks, and in the rest of our practice lives, let's see whether these three points are interesting to bring up: ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful.
Use whatever words are helpful to you.
Maybe "ardent" doesn't do it for me, but maybe you could say… we'll figure out what's a good translation for you.
That's an important process.
But it might be gentle energy, clarity, and mindfulness, or something.
Let's do some practice with the time remaining.
You will need, like last week, to have room to lie down.
There are stacks of mats all around, so maybe two mats together, the long way.
and once you've arranged that, and I think you need to really be flat this time, so not the zafu but two flat mats, once you've arranged that, please lie on your back.
That was all half an hour.
Very gentle posture.
It really does something, doesn't it, if you do it carefully, mindfully?
So I have two suggestions for you for the next week, if you'd like to try.
The first is, I made a recording of what we just did, a little bit longer.
It has two, actually, cleverly did two tracks.
The first track is introductory stuff, five or ten minutes, no, four or five minutes, which you might want to listen to once and then from then on skip.
And then there's a second track which is, I think, just exactly forty minutes of mindful movement, [unclear: "covert yoga"].
So what you could do is do that as many times as you have time for, or every day in a perfect world.
You could do that, or you could alternate that with the body scan recording.
That might be really interesting to do one day, the yoga or body scan in the morning.
You shouldn't do body scan in the evening, it appears.
Maybe do the body scan in the morning, yoga in the evening.
I don't know, you can try.
So that's the sort of formal practice suggestion.
And consider giving yourself permission to use whatever time you normally have set aside for sitting practice, to instead, for this time, devote it to that, just to see.
It has to do with the Buddha's strong recommendations that we study the temporariness of the body and dissolution of the body.
So there's a traditional Buddhist chant, Theravadan chant, a recitation, which I brought on a little card for you, and you could use this one of two ways.
One is just simply to recite this as part of your home practice, and let me tell you what it says.
These are the five daily reflections, and I'm not sure if they're canonical or just old tradition in Theravadan Buddhism, but you find them in Pali, so they're pretty old.
The five daily recollections are these.
They're not too cheerful, but they're important.
*I am of a nature to decay, I have not gone beyond decay.
I am of a nature to be diseased, I have not gone beyond disease.
I am of a nature to die, I have not gone beyond death.
All that is mine, dear and delightful, will change and vanish.*
*I am the owner of my karma, I am born of my karma, I am related to my karma, I live supported by my karma.
Any karma I will do, good or evil, that I will inherit.*
So karma here, you can just substitute action, if you don't know that word.
Karma means actions.
Maybe I should have translated it:
*I am the owner of my actions, I am born of my actions, I am related to my actions, I live supported by my actions.
Any actions I will do, good or evil, I will inherit the result.*
So you could do this just in home practice.
These kinds of things are a real different thing between running around saying, "Oh yeah, of course I know I'm going to die."
What are you talking about?
That's the one kind of understanding I don't have.
I did have one friend who was for a while convinced if he had the right herbs he would never die and never get sick.
Most of us, I think, don't think that way.
We understand that decay, disease and death are inevitable.
That's one kind of understanding, and what the Buddha is going after is a different, visceral understanding of the body.
To actually say that, and it's best to say it out loud, so hopefully you have a quiet place where you can say this out loud.
Three times is good.
So that's one way to use this.
Another way to use this, which really might be interesting, which I'm going to try, is go to the graveyard.
I actually mean this.
Go to the graveyard.

The Buddha had lots of recommendations to the monks to go to the graveyard, and in our graveyards we don't see bodies rotting there, but we know that we're in a graveyard, and there's the tombstone, and you have an idea in your mind that there's a person here, a decomposed person.
Go to the graveyard, and first just in some way pay respects to the person, whoever they were, and then you could just quietly read this, depending on the scene.
You don't want to act like you're doing something weird in the graveyard, but quietly read this to yourself, or say it out loud to yourself quietly.
You don't want anyone to feel like their relatives are being sort of used in some way, but we're there.

And then it might be further interesting to both go to a graveyard that's like somebody who lived a long life, and know it's not nice, and they're part of history, and you can relate to that and it feels okay to you to practice this there, but then also go to a child's grave.

Go to a grave where it doesn't feel right, it's not how it should be, it doesn't match, it makes us cry, and practice this there, and see that we have these categories and ways of thinking about death.
Death is okay to us only under certain circumstances, right, other circumstances not okay.
And those are two suggestions.
So, the yoga and the body scan and the five recollections, or just go about your business, and we'll see you later.
Let's close as we did last time, it's only three minutes after mine this time, with three prostrations with the Buddha, and the ancient chant in Pali for taking refuge.
